newsitem.title: USA: Great Western explores other banks - sources.
newsitem.headline: Great Western explores other banks - sources.

text.p: Great Western Financial Corp., the target of a $6.2 billion hostile takeover bid from H.F. Ahmanson and Co., is exploring alternative combinations with other potential bidders, sources said.
"Exploratory discussions are ongoing with more than one party," said a source close to Great Western.
"I'm aware there's a proactive interest among several other players, and it's my understanding there's been some dialogue between these players and Great Western," said another source.
Among those believed to have had contact with Great Western in recent days are First Bank System Inc., Washington Mutual and Norwest Corp.. All the banks declined comment.
Several analysts believe Seattle-based Washington Mutual is a prime candidate since it has expressed interest in the past to expand its franchise in California.
"I'm sure that Great Western has opened its books and is searching for the highest and most attractive bid for its shareholders," said Todd Pitsinger, analyst with Friedman, Billings and Ramsey.
"That's the fiduciary responsibilty of senior management and I believe it is being done in a timely matter," he said.
Analysts said NationsBank and KeyCorp are also potential rival bidders.

Great Western declined to comment beyond its statement Wednesday that it was reviewing Ahmanson's offer to swap 1.05 of its shares for each Great Western share, which valued Great Western stock at $44.50 a share, or $6.2 billion, on Thursday.
Ahmanson said the merger would save $400 million a year after closing about 200 branches in the combined system. Analysts estimate 2,500 jobs would be cut.

Ahmanson said all job losses related to the merger would be targeted to Great Western employees, prompting Great Western Chief Executive Officer John Maher to send a memo to employees Wednesday expressing his personal outrage.

Analysts believe Ahmanson's bid has put in play one of the few remaining valuable properties in the shrinking California savings and loan market and that higher bids from a rival as well as Ahmanson are likely.
"If anything, this bid has brought Great Western to the realisation that their days as an independent thrift are over," said Lloyd Greif, president of Greif & Co.

"If this moves to a competitive situation, there's a chance it could move the price up for Great Western. From Great Western's management's point of view, it would be a good thing to play it out a bit and get a better bid on the table," said Alison Davis, vice president for A.T. Kearney, a global management consultant firm.
But Davis and others said it will be hard for other players to top Ahmanson's synergies and cost savings due to its large market overlap with Great Western in southern California.

"Ahmanson's management team appears to be several months ahead of any other players in terms of really understanding their potential strategic and cost benefit from this deal and hence, others have a lot of work to do to catch up," said Davis.
